answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — an unsourced modern saying
answer.authorDates: popularly, but wrongly, pinned on Sun Tzu
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in no authentic translation of The Art of War — it is absent from Lionel Giles’ standard 1910 rendering, and Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” ↗ as contrary to Sun Tzu’s actual principles. No documented author — ancient or modern — has ever been tied to the line; it circulates as a self-help maxim under a borrowed name.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: Not found in the text; listed as misattributed

source.excerpt: Opportunities multiply as they are seized.
trail: The full text of Lionel Giles’ 1910 translation on Project Gutenberg ↗ contains neither “opportunities” nor “multiply” anywhere in it.
Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its “Misattributed” section, noting the opportunism it implies runs contrary to Sun Tzu’s emphasis on calculation and planning.
A longtime Art of War researcher lists it among invented Sun Tzu quotes ↗, tracing most such lines to mistranslation, film scripts, or fortune-cookie invention.
Popular repeaters such as Shortform ↗ assert it “comes from The Art of War” but cite no translation, chapter, or line.
source.excerptNote: Presented everywhere as a line from The Art of War, but no chapter, verse, or translation is ever cited — because the phrase is not in the book.

sourceLink.text: The Art of War, Lionel Giles translation (Project Gutenberg)

source.rightsNote: Because the wording matches no identifiable source — not Giles’ public-domain 1910 translation nor any other documented edition — its authorship and first publication are unknown, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. Sun Tzu’s original ancient text is long in the public domain, but that is not the source of this English sentence.

author.name: Sun Tzu
author.heading: About Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: c. 544–496 BC · Chinese general & strategist, traditional author of The Art of War
author.bio: Sun Tzu (Sunzi) is the semi-legendary Chinese military strategist traditionally credited with The Art of War, a compact treatise on strategy, deception, and terrain. Because his name carries ancient authority yet his text is terse and easy to paraphrase, he has become one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good business maxims he never wrote. This line is one of them: it reflects modern self-help optimism, not the calculating caution of his real work.

cite.sourceCitation: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, trans. Lionel Giles (London: Luzac & Co., 1910); full text at Project Gutenberg. The phrase “Opportunities multiply as they are seized” does not appear in this or any documented translation and is listed as misattributed on Wikiquote.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Sun Tzu. The line "Opportunities multiply as they are seized" appears in no authentic translation of The Art of War and is listed as misattributed on Wikiquote; its true origin is undocumented.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The sentence is offered as timeless battlefield wisdom, but it behaves like a modern motivational slogan wearing an ancient costume.

items.who: Sun Tzu / The Art of War
items.why: The phrase appears in no authentic translation. Lionel Giles’ standard 1910 English version — searchable in full on Project Gutenberg ↗ — contains neither “opportunities” nor “multiply.”
Wikiquote ↗ notes the opportunism the line celebrates conflicts with Sun Tzu’s stress on calculation, positioning, and winning before the battle — so even the sentiment is a poor fit.
Aggregators and blog posts assert it “comes from The Art of War” while a researcher who has spent years on the text lists it among invented Sun Tzu quotes ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no documented author for this line — ancient or modern. The honest answer is that it is an unsourced maxim floating under Sun Tzu’s name, and Wikiquote treats it as misattributed ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: Sun Tzu is a near-perfect host for orphan quotations: the real Art of War is ancient, revered in both military and business circles, and written in short, aphoristic lines that make almost any punchy sentence “sound like” it belongs. That combination lets a modern slogan borrow instant authority.

This particular line thrives in startup and productivity culture, where the message — act now, momentum compounds — is exactly what audiences want to hear. The absence of a chapter-and-verse citation goes unnoticed because the name alone does the persuading.
context.pull: A slogan borrowing an ancient name for authority it never earned.
